draft.title: Why Australians enlisted
card: When war broke out in 1914, Australia was part of the British Empire. Many Australians saw Britain as the mother country and felt a duty to help defend it.
Other reasons were personal. Some men wanted adventure and travel. Pay was also a pull, especially for men who were out of work.
Pressure from family, friends and the community pushed many men to join. Men who stayed home could be shamed for not going.
Some Aboriginal men enlisted too, even though rules meant to keep them out of the forces were in place. Some were accepted anyway, and some were turned away.
draft.remember: Men enlisted for many reasons: loyalty, adventure, pay and pressure. Some Aboriginal men joined despite the rules.

a.q: Tom, a farm worker in Victoria, joins up in 1914 because he believes Australians must stand by Britain. Which reason for enlisting is this?
opts: Loyalty to Britain
Hope of adventure
Need for regular pay
Pressure from friends
a.why: Tom acts out of a sense of duty to Britain, which many Australians saw as the mother country. It is not pressure from friends, because his reason is his own belief about Britain and not what others expect of him.
a.clue: Look at who Tom says Australians must stand by.

b.q: Jack, a young Aboriginal man in Victoria, is told in 1915 that he cannot join the army, but he enlists anyway. What does his case show?
opts: Some Aboriginal men enlisted despite rules to stop them
Rules kept every Aboriginal man out of the forces
Aboriginal men were not allowed to serve overseas
Aboriginal men enlisted only because they were paid more
b.why: The rules were meant to keep Aboriginal men out, but some still enlisted, so the rules did not stop everyone. The tempting option that rules kept every man out is wrong, because the card says some were accepted anyway.
b.clue: Did the rules stop every Aboriginal man from joining?

a.q: Tom's parents were born in England. In 1914 he joins up because he feels it is his own duty to help defend the land they came from. Which reason for enlisting is this?
opts: Loyalty to Britain
Hope of adventure
Need for regular pay
Pressure from family
a.why: Tom acts from his own sense of duty to defend England, part of Britain, which many Australians saw as the mother country. It is not pressure from family: his parents are only where his tie to Britain comes from, and nobody is pushing him to go.
a.clue: Is Tom acting on his own sense of duty, or on what others expect?

b.q: Jack, a young Aboriginal man in Victoria, is turned away at one recruiting office in 1915, but another office accepts him. What does his case show?
opts: Some Aboriginal men enlisted despite rules to stop them
Rules kept every Aboriginal man out of the forces
No rules applied to Aboriginal men who wanted to join
Rules forced Aboriginal men to join the forces
b.why: Rules were meant to keep Aboriginal men out, and Jack was turned away once, but he still got in, so the rules did not stop everyone. The tempting option that rules kept every Aboriginal man out is wrong, because the card says some were accepted anyway.
b.clue: Did the rules stop every Aboriginal man from joining?
